title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of fiber laser welded QP980/press-hardened 22MnB5 steel joint
abstract: Fiber laser welding of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel in butt configuration was performed in this study. The effect of heat input on microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of dissimilar joint was investigated. Laser power employed was varied from 1.6 to 2.4 kW while welding speed was kept constant at 2 m/min. The microstructure of fusion zone (FZ) was changed with the increasing laser power. Martensite and few bainite were observed when laser power ranged from 1.8 to 2.2 kW. Out of this range, the microstructure in FZ consisted of mixed structure of martensite and ferrite. Transformation from liquid phase to ferrite was promoted by Al-Si coating on the surface of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel. Heat affected zones (HAZs) of dissimilar joint were composed of martensite and bainite. Softened zone (SZ) appeared at the HAZ of 22MnB5 steel due to tempering behavior. The hardness of SZ and QP980 steel base metal declined with microstructure evolution. The fracture occurred at QP980 base metal when dissimilar joints were produced at laser power of 1.8 and 2.0 kW. When laser power reached 2.2 kW, the tensile samples failed at SZ owing to the increased softening degree. With further increasing laser power, the weakest region was FZ since ferrite declined the whole joint strength. A better Erichsen value was obtained at 2.0 kW (4.04 mm), which was balanced by more crash energy absorption and better deformation resistance.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Energy conservation requires sustainable development in the automotive industry. Automobile lightweight is a promising method for the reduction of fuel consumption. Steel structure still occupies an important role in material of body-in-white. Advanced high strength steels (AHSSs) can be utilized for thinner sheets structures without decreasing load-carrying capacity  [1,2] . QP980 steel is the new generation of AHSS employing quenching and partition (QP) process  [3] , which was designed for good strength and ductility. Boron alloy steel such as press-hardened 22MnB5 steel has been widely used in vehicle fabrication for its high strength, especially the bearing parts  [4] . The ultimate tensile strength of press-hardened 22MnB5 could reach 1500 MPa  [5,6] . Laser-welded blanks enable the joint of blanks with different mechanical properties, thickness or coating types. It achieves the flexible production and property control of specific area, which is becoming popular in automobile industry. The combination of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 could be expected to fulfill performance improvement in body-in-white. For instance, the B pillar (the vertical pillar between the front and rear doors of the car body) was composed of upper part requesting for ultrahigh strength and lower part requesting for better ductility. The QP980/press-hardened 22MnB5 steel welded joint can be applied to increase the overall mechanical performance.

At present, few researches focus on the laser welding of two types steel. Li et al.  [7]  investigated the microstructure evolution and formability of fiber laser welded QP980 steel joint. It was reported that failure of laser welded QP980 joint occurred at the base metal since the microstructure of FZ and HAZ was fully martensite with barely softening. Similar results were proved by Guo et al.  [8]  that the strength of laser welded QP980 steel joint was equivalent to the strength of base metal at different strain rates. Guo et al.  [9]  studied the dissimilar joint of QP980 steel and twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) steel. The results indicated that solidification cracks in the FZ was caused by the segregations, which reduced the strength of the whole joint. Jia et al.  [10]  welded QP980 steel to press-hardened 22MnB5 steel and investigated the microstructure evolution in HAZ of QP980 steel. The joints were produced at different welding speeds with constant laser power. Large window of welding speed provides optimal matching parameters. The effect of heat input on tensile behavior still needs further study because the large difference of heat input cannot make sure all the samples are in optimal conditions.

Press-hardened 22MnB5 steel faced problems of softening and coating removal during welding  [11–13] . The martensite structure in base metal could be softened when the temperature was ranged between tempered temperature and Ac 1  temperature. The soften area was reported to be ignored when the size was small enough, which depended on the heat input  [14] . Besides, press-hardened 22MnB5 steel was fabricated with Al-Si coating on the surface to avoid decarburization and oxidation during hot stamping process. The Al-Si coating could degrade the weldabilities of 22MnB5 steel by affecting the microstructure evolution  [15] . Saha et al.  [16]  studied the influence of Al-Si coating on laser welding of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel indicating that δ-ferrite formed in the FZ. The samples of tensile test failed at the FZ with declined strength. Kang et al.  [17]  investigated the microstructural changes and mechanical behavior of Al-Si coated press-hardened 22MnB5 welded joints. An increasing proportion of ferrite was found in FZ with deceasing laser power. The mechanical properties were deteriorated by the ferrite and intermetallic compounds formed at FZ and fusion boundary. Researchers discovered that Al element in the coating was mixed into the FZ during laser welding process enhancing the stability of ferrite, which could not be eliminated without special treatment  [18–20] . However, the proportion of ferrite could be controlled by the heat input during laser welding and hot stamping process  [17] . The microstructure evolution of laser welded QP980/press-hardened 22MnB5 steel joint is still not fully understood. For QP980 steel, the decomposition of retained austenite (RA) in HAZ might affect the strength. For press-hardened 22MnB5 steel, the Al-Si coating and decomposition of martensite may deteriorate the strength of FZ or SZ. All these problems are related to the heat input, which is of critical importance for controlling the mechanical behavior.

In this study, laser welding of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel was performed. The microstructure evolution and mechanical behavior of dissimilar joints obtained with different heat input were investigated. Characteristics of dissimilar welded joint including microstructure morphologies, microhardness, tensile behavior and Erichsen test were discussed in detail.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs:
1.2-mm thick QP980 steel sheets (supplied by TANGSTEEL Company, HBIS Group) and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel sheets (supplied by CHINA BAOWU STEEL GROUP) were selected as base metals in this study. The chemical compositions and tensile strength of the AHSSs base metals were listed in  Table 1 
                      .

The butt joint configuration in dimensions of 100 × 100 × 1.2 mm was adopted and welded by IPG YLS-6000 fiber laser system. Welding speed was fixed at 2 m/min to meet the efficiency requirements in industrial production. After preliminary trials, the laser power range was selected at 1.6–2.4 kW to match the welding speed. Out of this scope, the weld quality was reduced with presence of welding defects. Focused beam mode was employed and protective gas flow was 20 L/min in this study. The laser beam was focused on the central part where the base metal sheets were butted.

The typical cross sections of welded joints were cut perpendicularly to weld seam, and then grounded, polished and etched with 4% nital solution for 5−8 s. Microstructure was characterized by optical microscope and field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) equipped with an electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) to further identify the phase transformation.

The Vickers microhardness was measured under 500-g load with a dwell time of 15 s. The uniaxial tensile tests were tested by a universal INSTRON machine with 0.01 s −1  strain rate at room temperature. The tensile behavior was observed by a digital image correlation (DIC) Camera11-2M20G system to reveal the strain variation. Erichsen cupping tests were conducted with a hemisphere-shaped punch pushing on the weld seam. A blank holder force of 10 kN was applied on the samples to maintain the stability during tests. Geometry of the samples for tensile test and Erichsen cupping test are shown in  Fig. 1 
                       according to ASTM: E8 and ISO 20482 standard. The fracture morphologies after mechanical tests were observed via FE-SEM.

sections.heading: Microstructure of base metal
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 
                          shows microstructure morphologies of the QP980 steel and the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel base metals. In  Fig. 2 (a), a complex mixed structure containing martensite, ferrite and RA was observed in base metal of QP980 steel. Almost entire martensite structure was found in base metal of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel, as shown in  Fig. 2 (b).  Fig. 3 
                          shows the coating morphology of the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel. Based on the line-scanning results, two platforms with different Fe/Al atomic ratios could be observed and were identified as FeAl(Si) and Fe 2 Al 5  phases. Their crossing position might indicate the element change of α-Fe and base metal, which revealed that the Al-12 wt. %Si coating was transformed to Fe 2 Al 5  layer with FeAl(Si) phase and α-Fe layer after hot stamping process.

sections.heading: Weld morphology
paragraphs:
Fig. 4 
                          shows cross sections of laser welded QP980/press-hardened 22MnB5 steel joints produced at different laser powers. The dissimilar joints could be obtained in a relatively large processing window as shown in  Fig. 4 . At the low laser power of 1.6 kW, penetration was hard to be achieved and the defect occurred at the bottom of the weld seam due to insufficient heat input. Defect-free welded joints were produced when the laser power was ranged from 1.8 to 2.4 kW. The width of FZ and HAZ significantly increased due to increasing heat input. The shape of FZ was transformed from funnel shape to hourglass shape when heat input reached 2.0 kW. At 1.6 and 2.4 kW, a large volume fraction of white phase formed in the FZ, while only few comet-shaped white phases formed at the upper area of fusion boundary of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel side with laser powers of 1.8–2.2 kW.

sections.heading: Microstructure evolution
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          shows HAZ microstructure of laser welded QP980/22MnB5 steel joint produced at laser power of 2.0 kW. The microstructure evolution of joints obtained at all laser powers had the same trend, only the width of each zone changed. Hence, only one set of results was presented to avoid repetition. The HAZ region of QP980 steel contained two different sub-regions, namely coarse-grained HAZ and fine-grained HAZ as shown in  Fig. 5 (a) and (b). Martensite with few granular inclusions (EDS results show 23.42 at.% O, 0.11 at.% Al, and 76.47 at.% Fe) appeared while the austenite existed in base metal cannot be observed after welding. At the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel side, the HAZ was divided into coarse-grained HAZ, fine-grained HAZ and SZ. The microstructures of coarse-grained HAZ and fine-grained HAZ were composed of martensite and bainite, as shown in  Fig. 5 (c) and (d).  Fig. 5 (e) shows the microstructure of SZ. Martensite in the area of SZ experienced a maximum temperature above temper temperature but below the autenitizing temperature, which was partially decomposed to temper martensite. It was worth noting that the width of SZ increased with increasing laser power. The width of SZ produced from 1.6 to 2.4 kW was measured as 60, 150, 175, 190 and 235 μm, respectively.

Fig. 6 
                          shows SEM microstructure morphology of FZ in laser welded QP980/22MnB5 steel joints obtained at different laser powers. When the laser power was 1.6 kW, martensite, ferrite and RA were observed in the FZ as shown in  Fig. 6 (a). The white phase in  Fig. 4 (a) was identified as ferrite. When the laser power was ranged from 1.8 to 2.2 kW, the microstructures were transformed to martensite and bainite. No ferrite was observed in this case. However, the ferrite appeared again in the FZ when laser power reached 2.4 kW, as shown in  Fig. 6 (e). The results suggested that ferrite was formed at the low laser power of 1.6 kW or high laser power of 2.4 kW. Different microstructures formed in the FZ were attributed to the participation of partial Al-Si coating from press-hardened 22MnB5 steel surface. The content of Al element in the FZ was insufficient to generate intermetallic compounds according to previous study. Nevertheless, small content of Al element could enlarge the δ-ferrite proportion in Fe-Al binary system. The temperature range and the conversion ratio of the reaction from liquid phase to δ ferrite phase would be increased  [21,22] . Different microstructure evolution in the FZ occurred at laser power of 1.6 and 2.4 kW with involvement of Al element. For FZ of joint welded at 1.6 kW, large amount of ferrite was produced since relatively small volume in the FZ led to the increase of Al element concentration. The contribution of the Al element in accelerating the formation of ferrite became more obvious due to increased concentration. In  Fig. 6 (e), skeleton shaped ferrite was formed at the FZ of joint produced at 2.4 kW. The content of Al element in FZ did not increase when laser power ranged from 1.8 to 2.2 kW. The increasing heat input led to longer high temperature residence time, which provided more time for the reaction. More ferrite was transformed from liquid phase and could not fully convert to austenite in subsequent reaction.

To further study the influence of laser power and microstructural changes, FZ of welded joints produced at the range of 1.8–2.4 kW was tested using EBSD analysis.  Fig. 7 
                          shows results of inverse pole figure (IPF) and the kernal average misorientation (KAM) map at the center area of the FZ. The IPF reflected the crystal orientation. The KAM map represented the dislocation density. In  Fig. 7 (a), (c) and (e), no consistent orientation was founded in the FZ of joints welded at 1.8–2.2 kW. The grain size of martensite was determined by the prior austenite and had no significant variation. In the KAM map, joints obtained at laser power ranged from 1.8 to 2.2 kW also showed similar results. The martensite was transferred from austenite accompanied with crystal structure change, leading to high dislocations density. In  Fig. 7 (h), skeleton shaped ferrite was identified as blue area in KAM map, which represented a low level of dislocation density. The ferrite of the same color also had the consistent orientation as shown in IPF map of  Fig. 7 (g). This was because the ferrite with low dislocation density formed during laser welding process was δ-ferrite, which was precipitated before the martensite  [18] .

sections.heading: Microhardness profile
paragraphs:
The microhardness distribution across the QP980 steel/press-hardened 22MnB5 steel laser welded joint is shown in  Fig. 8 
                         . The hardness profile reflected the corresponding microstructure in FZ, HAZ and base metal of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel. Welded joints under different laser powers had the similar trend of microhardness distribution. The hardness of QP980 base metal was nearly 300 HV because of the mixed structure of martensite, ferrite and RA. The hardness of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel base metal was about 450 HV since the microstructure was composed of fully martensite as shown in  Fig. 2 (b). A relatively wide plateau of high hardness over 450 HV was observed at the FZ and HAZs of both QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel, owing to the fully martensite and bainite structure. With the increasing laser power, the overall hardness presented a downward trend due to coarser microstructure. At the FZ of joint produced at 2.4 kW, the hardness declined obviously due to the presence of ferrite structure. Note that the hardness of the SZ of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel was only approximately 280 HV, which was the softest area in the whole joint. However, no softening behavior was founded at the HAZ of QP980 steel side. The tempering of martensite in HAZ of QP980 steel could be ignored since the softened zone was narrow in laser welded QP980 steel joint  [8] . In this study, the softening of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel was related to its martensite structure and consistent with related research  [13] . The narrow SZ in the joint caused inhomogeneous mechanical properties in the weld joint and affected the performance.

sections.heading: Tensile behavior
paragraphs:
Fig. 9 
                          presents the stress-strain curve and fracture location of samples produced with laser power ranging from 1.6 to 2.4 kW. The failure location was changed with variation of heat input. The results of tensile tests suggested that samples with laser power of 1.6 kW failed at FZ with tensile strength of 280 MPa. The incomplete penetration welding defect led to insufficient bearing area. When the heat input reached the range of 1.8–2.0 kW, tensile test samples performed optimal tensile strength over 1050 MPa. The failure position was at the base metal of QP980 steel because the mixed structure of ferrite and martensite in the QP980 base metal had lower strength than entire martensite structure in FZ and HAZs  [23] . The elongation also reached the maximum value of 12%, which was lower than that of standard QP980 steel tensile test samples, since the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel side provided few deformations. When the sample was produced at 2.2 kW, the failure location was at SZ of 22MnB5 steel. Tensile strength and elongation dropped to 850 MPa and 7.8%, respectively. With the increasing heat input, samples produced at 2.4 kW failed at FZ with tensile strength of 724 MPa. Based on the analysis above, the QP980 steel base metal and SZ at press-hardened 22MnB5 side were the most possible failure positions of the tensile test samples.

Fig. 10 
                          shows the DIC results related to the investigated deformation during tensile test. Different stages with intervals of 25 s in the joints welded at 2.0 kW ( Fig. 10 (a)) and 2.2 kW ( Fig. 10 (b)) were captured to compare the global strain during tensile test. When laser power was 2.0 kW, the strain concentrated on the QP980 base metal. The HAZ of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel is slightly deformed before the fracture of QP980 steel base metal. When laser power was 2.2 kW, the initial strain also accumulated at the QP980 base metal and then the SZ started deforming. The difference was that the SZ became the deformation zone in the next stage of the tensile test.

The joint performances and changes in fracture location with variation of laser powers were determined by the microstructure evolution. The deterioration in mechanical properties of joint produced at 2.4 kW was caused by the ferrite formed at FZ. However, softening occurred at all the conditions. Although the SZ had low microhardness and deformation during the tensile test, the failure only occurred at SZ when the laser power was 2.2 kW. When the laser power were 1.8 kW and 2.0 kW, failure locations were transferred to QP980 base metal.  Fig. 11 
                          shows the stress state schematic of laser welded dissimilar joint. At the side of QP980 steel, both HAZ and base metal suffered only one stress along the tensile direction. However, the HAZ and base metal at press-hardened 22MnB5 steel side were both composed of martensite with high strength. The narrow SZ was restrained by HAZ and base metal during the tensile test. Deformation in the SZ created stress σ 1  in the tensile direction, σ 2  in transverse direction and σ 3  in radial direction. Thus, three-dimensional stress condition was applied on the SZ. The radial stress σ 3  was ignored since the sample was thin. σ 2  perpendicular to the stretching direction was added on the SZ besides the σ 1  along the stretching direction. For area of QP980 side, the actual stress was equivalent to σ 1 . Similar phenomenon was proved in studies of high strength steel welding  [24] . The actual stress σ e  of the SZ can be calculated by the following formula.  
                            
                               (1) 
                               σ e  = ((1/2) {[(σ 1  −σ 2 ) 2  + (σ 2  −σ 3 ) 2  + (σ 1  −σ 3 ) 2 ]} 1/2 
                               
                            
                         σ 3  was the radial stress and could be treated as zero value in this condition. The actual stress σ e  applied on SZ was lower than the σ 1  applied on QP980 base metal. The SZ at press-hardened 22MnB5 steel side performed better strength than QP980 base metal at laser powers of 1.8 and 2.0 kW. With the increase of the laser power, an enhanced softening reduced the bearing capacity of SZ. Meanwhile, the restrain effect was weakened by the wider size of SZ. The failure position was at SZ due to its deteriorative tensile strength.

Fig. 12 
                          shows the fractography of tensile samples produced at different laser powers. In  Fig. 12 (a) and (b), the fracture of joints obtained at 1.8 and 2.0 kW presented typical ductile fracture characteristics. Dimples could be observed all over the fracture surface.  Fig. 12 (c) is the fractography of tensile samples welded at 2.2 kW. The fracture of SZ had a characterization of both brittle and ductile fracture with some shallow dimples. The fracture of samples obtained at 2.4 kW presented typical brittle fracture. The river pattern could be observed at the magnified area, which also demonstrated poor mechanical properties as reported in previous study  [19] .

sections.heading: Formability
paragraphs:
Figs. 13 and 14  
                         
                         display results of Erichsen cupping test, which further identified the formability of the welded joints. Welded joints produced at 1.6 and 2.4 kW were not considered since defects could be observed in the macro-morphology of the weld seam. The Eirichsen values of joints produced at 1.8, 2.0 and 2.2 kW were 2.85, 4.04 and 3.20 mm, respectively. Corresponding maximum loads of samples fabricated with laser powers of 1.8, 2.0 and 2.2 kW, and obtained from the displacement and load curve of Erichsen cupping test in  Fig. 14 , were 7.9, 17.2 and 10.7 kN, respectively. The optimal results were obtained at 2.0 kW while the failure occurred at the SZ along the welding direction. QP980 base metal and SZ had the lowest tensile strength. However, it was more difficult for the SZ to deform in multiple directions due to its poor ductility and restraint at both ends. In other cases, the fusion boundary became the failure position with low Enrichsen value. This was attributed to the cometary white ferrite phase formed at the fusion boundary as shown in  Fig. 4 (b) and (d). The formability was determined by multiple factors. A further explanation of this phenomenon is underway.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this study, laser welding of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel was performed. The microstructure and mechanical behavior of laser welded joints produced at different laser powers were investigated. The main conclusions were summarized as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Appropriate laser power range for welding was 1.8–2.4 kW when welding speed was fixed at 2 m/min. Incomplete penetration of the joint occurred when laser power was low while over penetration was observed when laser power was high. Welded joints were divided into FZ and HAZ. The shape of FZ transformed from funnel shape at 1.8 kW to hourglass shape at 2.0 kW. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Martensite and bainite were obtained in the FZ and two HAZs of QP980 steel and press-hardened 22MnB5 steel of joints produced at all welding conditions. For joint welded at 2.4 kW, continuously distributed ferrite was formed due to involvement of Al-12 wt.%Si coating of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel. At the HAZ boundary of press-hardened 22MnB5 steel, SZ appeared and was mainly composed of martensite and tempered martensite. Softening size and degree increased with increasing laser power. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The welded joints failed at the QP980 steel base metal achieving the highest ultimate tensile strength (1050 MPa) when the laser powers were ranged from 1.8 to 2.0 kW. However, joint welded at 2.2 kW fractured at the SZ of the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel as it became the weakest region. When the laser power reached 2.4 kW, the ferrite formed in FZ leads to an early failure. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            When the joint was welded at the laser power of 2.0 kW, Erichsen test samples failed at the SZ of the press-hardened 22MnB5 steel having the highest Erichsen values (4.4 mm) and peak load (17.2 kN). The Erichsen value of joint welded at 1.8 and 2.2 kW were significantly decreased.
